title: Should the town hire a consultant to review its employee housing rules?
body:
Town Council is expected to discuss bringing in consulting services for a comprehensive review of Telluride's employee rental housing policies. That sounds procedural — until you think about what it means.

Some residents will say outside expertise is exactly what's needed: fresh eyes, no local politics, a real audit of whether the rules are working. Others will push back — consultants cost money, and the people who know how employee housing actually functions up here are already in town.

Is outside help the right move for something this local?

title: A trail, a canopy, and a fresh coat for the jail
body:
The Planning Commission has a mixed plate: a connector trail, a fuel island canopy, and painting the county jail are all on the table. Each one sounds routine until you think about what it competes with. Trail access is something a lot of people here care about. Jail upkeep is a public obligation. A fuel canopy is infrastructure. The question is whether these get weighed against each other — or just rubber-stamped one by one.

Which of these would you most want the commission to slow down and scrutinize?

title: Who gets to pour — and who decides?
body:
The Liquor Licensing Authority meets to act on license applications or modifications for local establishments. A hearing officer presides, but new licenses require Town Council approval on top of that — and state sign-off too. Some residents think layered oversight protects the character of a small town. Others figure it slows things down and adds hoops for businesses that already face long odds up here. Both camps have a point.

So where do you land — is multi-level liquor licensing oversight the right call for Telluride, or is it more process than the situation warrants?
choices: State plus town is about right

title: The county wants a housing action plan
body:
The Board of County Commissioners is set to consider creating a housing action plan at its November 18 meeting. No details on what that plan would contain are available yet — it's still a proposal.

That's where the tension lives. Some residents will say a formal plan is long overdue and that without one, housing decisions stay reactive. Others will wonder whether another plan just produces a document that sits on a shelf while the actual problem doesn't move.

So — does a housing action plan change anything, or is the county already past the point where planning helps?

title: Who reviews the rent rules — and does it matter who does it?
body:
Council is moving toward hiring outside consultants to do a comprehensive review of Telluride's employee rental housing policies. Some residents will see that as a smart move — fresh eyes, no local baggage, a real audit of whether the policies are actually working. Others will push back: local housing is a local problem, and paying consultants to study it can feel like a way to delay hard decisions the town already has the information to make. No contract has been approved yet — this is still at the discussion stage.

So where do you land: is outside expertise the right tool here, or is this one the town should work out itself?

title: Should the county have an AI policy — and what should it say?
body: Commissioners are expected to dig into a draft AI resolution and policy, alongside Senate Bill 26-189, at a work session. It's not a final vote — just a conversation. But the tension is real. Some residents will want the county ahead of this, with clear rules before AI tools become routine in government work. Others will wonder why a small mountain county needs a formal AI policy at all, or worry that outside legislation like SB 26-189 is already doing the steering for them. Where do you come down?
choices: Get the policy in place now
Overkill for a county this size
Let the state law handle it

title: One deed restriction, one exception request
body:
The Board of County Commissioners, sitting as the Housing Authority, will consider an exception request from Esperanza Reyes to continuing residency and employment standards under her deed restriction. Deed restrictions on affordable units exist for a reason — they keep housing in local hands over time. But life doesn't always fit the rules: circumstances change, and a flat denial can feel punishing. Some neighbors will say exceptions undermine the whole system. Others will say a case-by-case review is exactly how fair administration works.

Where do you come down — should deed restriction exceptions be granted case by case, or held firm?

title: Gas-powered leaf blowers — next to go?
body: The Ecology Commission is set to review a proposed ordinance that would phase out combustion-powered lawn and garden equipment. Up here, that means gas blowers, trimmers, mowers — the whole category. Supporters will say it's overdue: cleaner air, quieter streets, fewer fumes in a canyon that traps everything. Skeptics will push back on who actually bears the cost — landscapers and contractors switching equipment mid-career aren't absorbing that lightly. Nothing is adopted yet; this is still a review. So: is a phase-out of gas lawn equipment a reasonable next step, or an overreach?

title: Deck repairs — or something more?
body: The Design Review Board has a work session coming up on deck repairs and possible extensions at 120 Vischer Dr. Work sessions are exploratory — nothing's decided yet. But that phrase "possible extensions" is where opinions tend to split. Some neighbors see deck work as routine upkeep that keeps older structures sound. Others worry that a repair conversation quietly becomes an expansion conversation, adding mass or footprint to something that wasn't originally sized for it. Where's the line between fixing what's there and changing what's there?

title: How many boards does it take to hire one consultant?
body: The Planning & Zoning Commission is holding a special meeting to discuss a Request for Proposal for consulting services to review Telluride's employee rental housing policies. It's also on the agenda — in the same week — for the Housing Authority Subcommittee, the Arts & Special Events Commission, Town Council budget talks, and the Ecology Commission. Some residents will see that as thorough, multi-angle vetting before anything changes. Others will wonder why so many boards are weighing in before a consultant is even hired. Who actually drives this process — and does spreading it across this many tables help or slow things down?
choices: Just hire someone and move on

title: One lot line erased on W. Columbia
body:
A minor subdivision application for 510 W Columbia Avenue would vacate the lot line between two existing parcels and merge them into a single roughly 5,625-square-foot lot — Lot 40R. Straightforward on paper. But combining parcels can change what's buildable, and neighbors tend to notice when a lot suddenly has more room to work with. Some will see a reasonable consolidation of property a landowner already holds. Others will wonder what comes next on a freshly enlarged footprint.

What's your read — routine paperwork, or does it matter?

title: A height variance before it's built
body:
The Design Review Board is taking up a height variance request for an undeveloped lot on Mountain Village Blvd. Nothing's approved yet — it's on the agenda, not in the books.

That's where the split usually starts. One side figures variances on empty lots are exactly the right moment to ask: before anything goes up, before neighbors are staring at it. The other side worries that granting height exceptions on undeveloped land sets a precedent that quietly rewrites what the rules actually mean.

So — is a pre-construction variance the responsible time to be flexible, or the riskiest?
choices: Best time to bend the rules

title: Should an outside consultant rewrite the housing rules?
body:
The Telluride Housing Authority Subcommittee is set to discuss a request for proposals to hire outside consulting services for a comprehensive review of the town's employee rental housing policies. That means fresh eyes — but also outside hands — on rules that shape who gets to live up here and under what terms.

Some will see it as overdue: policies calcify, and an independent review could surface fixes insiders are too close to see. Others will wonder whether handing that work to consultants risks losing the local knowledge — and accountability — that should drive housing decisions.

So: is outside expertise the right tool for this, or should the community be leading its own review?

title: Pause the open space fund — or hold the line?
body:
Council is taking up an ordinance that would suspend the 5% capital fund allocation for open space in 2027. It's a first reading, so nothing is decided yet. The argument for: the town is facing budget pressure, and a one-year pause buys room to maneuver. The argument against: open space protection is exactly what gets quietly eroded during tight years, and a suspension sets a precedent. Both sides have a point.

So — is one year off a reasonable trade-off, or does pausing the open space fund open a door that's hard to close?
choices: One year is fine, budgets are tight
Don't touch the open space fund
Sets a bad precedent either way

title: Should someone outside town hall review the housing rules?
body:
Multiple boards — the Housing Authority Subcommittee, Planning & Zoning, the Arts & Special Events Commission, and the Town Council budget session — are all being asked to weigh in on hiring outside consultants to do a comprehensive review of Telluride's employee rental housing policies. That's a lot of simultaneous attention on one question.

Some residents will see outside eyes as overdue — fresh perspective on rules that may have calcified. Others will wonder why the town needs to pay consultants to evaluate programs that local staff and elected boards already know inside out.

So: does a third-party review of workforce housing policy sound like a good use of town resources to you — or not?

title: Two nights of concerts in Town Park — good idea?
body: Council is looking at a proposed two-night concert in Town Park for August 2027. Up here, Town Park events are a long-running argument: they bring energy and economic life, and they also bring noise, crowds, and wear on a space that neighbors actually live next to. Supporters will say it's part of what makes this place tick. Skeptics will say two nights is one more than the canyon needs. Nothing's been decided — this is still a review stage. So: how do you feel about adding another multi-night concert to Town Park?

title: Should a Veteran's Flag fly at the 4-H Event Center?
body:
The Board of County Commissioners is expected to decide whether to hang a Veteran's Flag at the 4-H Event Center. Sounds simple. But these calls rarely are — some residents will see it as a straightforward act of recognition, long overdue. Others may wonder about precedent: once one flag goes up, what comes next, and who decides? Public comment is on the agenda, so the board wants to hear from people before the vote.

Where do you come down on it?

title: The gondola update nobody's agreed on yet
body:
The Gondola Sub Committee meets to hear an update on the FTA Capital Investment Program — federal transit money that could move the Telluride-Mountain Village gondola project forward. Some residents see a federally backed gondola connection as the right answer to traffic and parking up here. Others wonder whether chasing federal capital funding means ceding control, adding complexity, or committing to a project before the community has fully weighed in. Nothing's been decided — this is an update, not a vote.

So where do you stand: is federal investment in the gondola a good path forward, or does it give you pause?

title: One lot line goes away in West Telluride
body:
A minor subdivision application for 510 W Columbia Avenue is headed to the Planning & Zoning Commission Chair. The proposal would vacate the lot line between two existing parcels and combine them into a single lot — roughly 5,625 square feet — to be known as Lot 40R.

Straightforward paperwork to some. To others, consolidating lots in a tight mountain town raises a familiar question: does merging parcels quietly remove a future opportunity for more housing, or is private owners managing their own property simply nobody else's business?

What do you think — does a lot-line vacation like this matter to the broader community, or is it a private decision that doesn't warrant much scrutiny?

title: Merge EMS and Ridgway Fire — or keep them separate?
body: Commissioners are sitting down to talk about a potential merger between EMS and Ridgway Fire services. There's a preliminary draft agreement on the table, along with budget and operational questions. Consolidation backers tend to argue it stretches resources further and streamlines response. Critics worry that merging two distinct cultures and service areas creates more problems than it solves — and that "preliminary" can become fait accompli fast. Nothing's been decided; this is a work session. So: does combining these services sound like smart regionalism to you, or a deal that deserves a harder look first?

title: Shandoka lot: what goes there?
body:
The Planning & Zoning Commission is holding a public hearing on the Shandoka Lot Redevelopment Project — specifically a Preliminary Planned Unit Development application. A PUD gives developers flexibility to shape density and use in ways standard zoning might not allow. That's the tension. Some residents see PUDs as a practical tool for getting housing and mixed uses into tight spots. Others see them as a workaround that lets projects exceed what the neighborhood signed up for. Nothing is decided yet — this is a hearing, not a final vote.

What's your read on PUD redevelopment in town: reasonable flexibility or too much room to maneuver?

title: Mountain Village wants to expand the post office — and a few other things
body: The TMVOA board is set to consider a Mountain Village Post Office expansion, among other items — Plaza Guest Services funding, Conference Center Plaza enhancements, a Telluride Arts grant request, and a feasibility analysis for Lots 1007/1008. That's a lot on one agenda. The post office question alone tends to split people: some see expansion as overdue infrastructure for a growing resident base, others wonder whether the space and money could go toward more pressing needs like workforce housing — which also gets a working group recap at this meeting. What should be the board's actual priority right now?

title: A trail through Lawson Hill — what's the cost of connection?
body: The Open Space Commission is expected to take up the Lawson Hill Connector Trail Project, with proposals currently being sought. On the surface it sounds straightforward — more trail, more access. But connector trails through open space tend to split people. Some see a long-overdue link that makes the area more usable for more residents. Others worry about what more foot traffic does to land that was set aside precisely to limit it. Neither side is wrong, exactly. So: is a connector trail through open space a win for the community, or a compromise of what open space is for?

title: Should employee housing policy get a consultant?
body:
Town Council is taking up a request for proposals to hire a consultant to review Telluride's employee rental housing policies. On one hand, outside expertise might spot gaps locals are too close to see — employee housing is a chronic pressure up here and the stakes are real. On the other hand, some residents will ask why the town needs to pay a consultant to study a problem the community already lives every day, and whether the money and time could go straight to solutions instead.

So: is bringing in outside help on employee housing policy a smart move, or a detour?

title: The county wants to paint the jail. Also: helium.
body: The Board of County Commissioners has a full plate this week — material hauling, trail construction, a fuel island canopy, jail painting, and a multi-jurisdictional hazard mitigation plan update. Tucked in alongside all that is an ECMC violation order against American Helium Operating LLC. That last one is easy to scroll past, but a state enforcement action against an energy operator in the county tends to land differently depending on who you ask. Some residents see resource extraction as a threat to the land and water up here. Others see it as legitimate economic activity the county shouldn't be in the business of cheering or jeering. The board hasn't taken a public position. So — how much does an energy violation order on the county's agenda matter to you?
choices: It's a state issue, not ours

title: Wildfire code is now law — what comes next?
body:
Town Council adopted the Colorado Wildfire Resiliency Code amendment to the Land Use Code back in August 2026. Now Planning & Zoning is expected to work through what implementation actually looks like. That's where it gets interesting. Some folks figure tighter building standards protect the whole community — a fire doesn't ask whose roof it jumps to next. Others worry the new rules add cost and friction to construction that's already brutal up here. The code is adopted, but the details aren't settled yet.

So: do you think the wildfire code amendment will make Telluride meaningfully safer, or mostly make building harder?

title: Paper bills now cost extra — worth it?
body: Buried in a canceled-meeting notice: San Miguel Power Association is adding a new fee for paper billing. If you want a bill in the mail, you'll pay extra for it. The case for it is straightforward — digital is cheaper, and costs get passed to everyone otherwise. The case against it is just as real — not everyone is set up for online billing, and fees like this tend to land hardest on folks least able to absorb them. So: is a paper billing fee a reasonable nudge, or does it leave some neighbors behind?

title: Leak forgiveness — fair relief or a slippery slope?
body:
The Norwood Water Commission has four residential leak forgiveness requests on its October 13 agenda — customers on Hwy 145, Summit St, Juniper, and Grand Ave asking for relief on their bills. The case for: leaks happen, the water's already gone, and a punishing bill doesn't undo it. The case against: forgiveness spreads the cost across everyone else on the system, and the 2027 budget and 2025 audit are both on the same agenda, with water system costs still climbing. Where's the line between neighbor helping neighbor and just shifting the tab?

Should a water commission grant leak forgiveness, or is that a cost the customer has to own?

title: Beavers on the agenda
body:
Town Council is set to take up a draft Beaver Management Plan. Up here, that lands differently for different people. Beavers reshape water flow, build habitat, and can also flood irrigation ditches, damage culverts, and complicate infrastructure. Some residents see them as a net good — natural engineers in a drought-stressed landscape. Others want the town to manage them aggressively before the damage stacks up. A draft plan means choices are coming, but nothing is decided yet.

Where do you come down: let the beavers work, or get ahead of the problems they cause?

title: The county's hazard plan is up for a rewrite — does yours match theirs?
body: The Board of County Commissioners is taking up a multi-jurisdictional hazard mitigation plan update alongside procurement for trail construction, material hauling, a fuel island canopy, and jail painting. Hazard mitigation plans are meant to coordinate how different agencies respond when things go sideways — floods, fires, the usual up here. Some residents think regional coordination is exactly what's needed. Others wonder whether a multi-jurisdictional plan papers over the gaps between agencies more than it closes them. Nothing is final yet — this is still at the Board level. So: do coordinated regional hazard plans actually make communities safer, or do they spread responsibility thin?
